sections.html:
Habersham County sits in the Blue Ridge of northeast Georgia. Clarkesville is the seat and Cornelia is the biggest city. The 2020 count was 46,031 residents, and the July 2025 estimate of 50,416 means growth of 9.5%. About 20.3% of residents are 65 or older.

Owner-occupants hold close to three of every four homes, and 390 permits in 2025 show new building joining a digest of mostly older property. The appraisal staff sets values using recent sales and market conditions on January 1, so a house's figure can follow neighborhood sales.

sections.h2: Who does what in Habersham County property tax
sections.html:
The tax commissioner holds an elected constitutional office. It sends bills, collects, accounts for and disburses the money, and takes no part in setting values or rates. Values are the job of the Board of Tax Assessors, which has had five members since January 1, 1990, each serving a three-year term. Rates are set by the county commissioners and the school board, while the state's own levy cannot go beyond one-fourth of a mill.

  • Tax commissioner: 130 Jacobs Way, Suite 202, Clarkesville, GA 30523, phone (706) 839-0120, open on weekdays from 8:00 until 4:45, with Saturdays closed until further notice.
  • Tax assessors: phone (706) 839-0100, which is also the number for mobile home registration questions.
  • Board of Tax Assessors meetings: second and fourth Mondays monthly, beginning at 9 a.m.

The assessors' board decides which properties are exempt, approves or denies Conservation Use applications and homestead exemptions, reviews tax returns, and levies penalties against property that was never returned. It also meets with taxpayers to talk through concerns, so a seller who doubts a value can ask for that conversation before listing.

Further detail sits on the commissioner's information page and the assessors' board page.

sections.h2: Due dates for real property and mobile homes
sections.html:
Bills are mailed by August 15 and payment is due November 15 of the same year. That is earlier than the state default of December 20. Mobile and modular homes run on a different cycle. Their bills usually go out around February 1, and the tax and location permit are tied to April 1.

Missing the April 1 payment and permit on a mobile home brings a 10% penalty, a citation to appear in the county's Magistrate Court, and possibly a sale of the home. A decal has to be displayed, and registration is done through the assessors' office.

The commissioner's office is the place to confirm what you owe, since it bills and collects for every taxing body on the parcel. Ask for the figure by parcel, and ask what the bill covers so you can tell the county, school and state portions apart. If the bill seems off, call the assessors at (706) 839-0100 about the value rather than the commissioner, who cannot change it.

When you plan to sell between mailing and the due date, ask whether the bill has been issued yet. Settlement agents usually want proof of payment or a payoff letter, so keep the receipt where you can find it.

Assessment notices normally arrive in spring. An owner who disagrees has 45 days from the date on the notice. The written appeal may argue taxability, value, uniformity or a refused exemption, and it goes to the Board of Tax Assessors naming the method you pick.

Mobile homes carry an extra step. If the owner still disagrees after a changed value, an appeal to the Board of Equalization can follow within 21 days of that notice. That board is appointed by the grand jury and hears administrative appeals from the assessors' values. For a regular parcel, ask the assessors' office for forms and the exact sequence.

Bring comparable sales, photos and any repair estimates, since the board works from market conditions on January 1.

The Tax Assessor's office handles homestead applications, and new buyers should carry in the warranty deed. Filing by April 1 covers your first claimed year, and a late filing slides to the following year. After approval the exemption renews itself until your residence, ownership or qualifying category changes. Local exemptions replace state ones whenever the local amount is greater.

  • Land in genuine agricultural use can be assessed at 30% rather than 40% of fair market value.
  • Conservation Use valuation is granted in return for a covenant with the assessors to keep the land in qualifying use for ten years at least.
  • Freeport exemption for manufacturers can reach three categories: raw goods, goods being processed, and finished goods held in a warehouse for out-of-state shipment. Applications are filed between January 1 and April 1.
  • A business's equipment, machinery and fixtures are assessed at 40% of fair market value.

sections.h2: What the assessors can do for a seller
sections.html: The Board of Tax Assessors meets on the second and fourth Mondays and talks through concerns with taxpayers. A seller who thinks the value runs high can bring recent sales and ask how the figure was reached before the appeal clock matters. Do this early in the year, because the 45 days run from the notice date and are short once the notice arrives.

sections.h2: Selling when tax is still due
sections.html:
Georgia holds the January 1 owner responsible for the whole year and refunds nothing for a partial year. The sale contract normally decides who actually pays, so begin by learning the precise balance.

Phone the tax commissioner at (706) 839-0120 and ask what the parcel owes for this year and any before it. When closing lands between the August mailing and the November 15 date, tell the closing agent whether the new bill has gone out and been paid. A mobile home bill follows the April 1 cycle and stands apart from real property. A homestead exemption ends when you move or ownership changes, so tell the assessors after you leave and let the buyer file separately.

A few calls early on keep a closing on schedule. Ask the commissioner for the balance on every year, not only the current one. Ask the assessors whether your homestead and any Conservation Use covenant are on file, because a buyer of farmland will want to know whether the covenant continues. Gather the assessment notice, the latest bill, and the warranty deed for your own records.

If you own a mobile home, confirm that its tax, permit and decal are current before an offer arrives. A cash buyer who closes quickly still depends on clean tax records, so paying any open balance from your proceeds at the table is the usual route. The payoff letter from the commissioner is the document your closing agent will ask for.

faqs.q: What day is Habersham County property tax due?
faqs.a: Bills are mailed by August 15 and payment is expected by November 15. For mobile and modular homes, bills typically go out near February 1 and the tax is tied to April 1.

faqs.q: Where do I find the Habersham County tax commissioner?
faqs.a: The main office is at 130 Jacobs Way, Suite 202, Clarkesville, GA 30523, phone (706) 839-0120. Weekday hours run from 8:00 to 4:45, and Saturdays are closed until further notice.

faqs.q: What is the time limit to appeal a Habersham County value?
faqs.a: You have 45 days from the date on the notice. A written appeal naming your chosen method goes to the Board of Tax Assessors.

faqs.q: By when must a Habersham County homestead application arrive?
faqs.a: April 1 in the first year you claim. Take the application to the Tax Assessor's office, with your warranty deed if the purchase is recent.

faqs.q: Is farmland taxed differently in Habersham County?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Qualifying agricultural property is assessed at 30% of fair market value, not 40%, and Conservation Use valuation applies current-use value in exchange for a covenant of ten years or longer with the assessors.
